vignette: The convoy rolls through the fractured valley when the first mortars land. He is twenty-six, traveling as a relief worker, and the earth jumps beneath his boots. Tires blow. Concrete dust chokes the air, thick with the sharp scent of cordite. He drags a medic behind a collapsed storefront, watching the man's breathing grow ragged, then stop. He presses himself against wet brick until the shelling fades, his heart hammering like a trapped bird. He tells me he never made a sound. He just waited. He returns home two years later, trades his canvas rucksack for a leather apron, and takes a position at a quiet jewelry studio downtown. At twenty-eight, he settles into a solitary apartment, far from neighbors he rarely meets. The work demands steady hands, magnifying loupes, and a deliberate slowness he craves. He sets stones, files edges, solders clasps. The loupe rests against his right eye, narrowing the world to a circle of controlled light. But the control is brittle. When a delivery cart backfires on the street below, his body jerks upright, fingers curling into fists before he forces them to relax. He checks the shop's front window three times before closing. He sleeps on the couch, mattress pulled from the bedroom after he stops waking up gasping, convinced the ceiling is cracking open. He moves through his days with a careful economy, eating at the same café, sitting in the same corner booth, keeping his phone face-down. He tells me he feels detached from his own hands, as if they belong to someone who knows how to survive what he survived. The gold he polishes shines, but it feels cold. He avoids news reports, stops answering calls from his old coordination contacts, and finds himself tracing the edges of his workbench when panic rises, grounding himself in the familiar weight of steel tweezers. He says he wants to be present, but his attention keeps fracturing, pulling him backward into the smoke, the weight of a duffel bag he had to drop to run, the silence that followed. Now, at twenty-nine, he sits across from me. He watches the dust motes drift in the afternoon light, his breath shallow, as if counting the seconds between them. He adjusts his posture, the micro-tremor in his shoulders familiar to me by now. He speaks in measured phrases, choosing each word as carefully as he once chose which supplies to save. The shop bell still makes him flinch when he visits to pick up client orders. He leaves earlier now, parking a block away, walking the perimeter of the neighborhood before stepping inside. He doesn't know how to stop waiting for the ground to shake. He just keeps setting stones, one at a time, trying to build something steady out of what he can hold.
